subject: Cloud Computing
title: CDNs: Content Closer to You
description: Learn CDNs: Content Closer to You in one minute.

hook.text: A user in Tokyo requests a video hosted in Virginia. That's 6,700 miles of latency.

buildup.text: A CDN caches copies of content on servers around the world, close to where users actually are.

discovery.text: When Tokyo requests that video, the CDN serves it from a nearby server — maybe in Osaka.

twist.text: CDNs handle over half of all internet traffic today. Without them, the web would feel painfully slow.

climax.text: Cloudflare, Akamai, and AWS CloudFront are the invisible layer that makes the internet feel fast.

punchline.text: CDNs don't speed up the internet. They shorten the distance.

quiz.question: How does a CDN improve website performance?
options: By caching content on servers closer to users geographically
By compressing all files to 1% of their original size
By upgrading users' internet connections automatically

details.summary: Content delivery networks cache copies of static content at edge locations worldwide, serving files from the location nearest to each user. CDNs dramatically reduce latency for images, videos, and scripts while offloading traffic from origin servers.
details.whyItMatters: CDNs make websites and applications feel fast for users everywhere, regardless of where the origin server is located. They are essential for any application serving a global audience.
takeaways: CDNs cache content at hundreds of global edge locations
Users get content from the nearest edge, reducing latency
CDNs reduce origin server load and bandwidth costs

faq.question: How much do CDNs improve performance?
faq.answer: CDNs can reduce page load times by 50 percent or more for geographically distant users. Instead of crossing continents to reach an origin server, content is served from an edge location often within the same city. This reduces latency from hundreds of milliseconds to single digits.

faq.question: What content works best with CDNs?
faq.answer: Static content like images, CSS, JavaScript, videos, and downloads benefit most from CDN caching. Dynamic content can also be accelerated through CDN features like connection optimization and edge computing. CDNs are less useful for highly personalized, uncacheable responses.
